# Notes on the Basement Flood

Water came up through the floor drain around two in the morning. Not a trickle — an inch, then two, then it stopped rising around dawn. I didn't hear it happen. The dog did; she wouldn't go downstairs for three days afterward, and honestly? Neither did I, not until the insurance adjuster forced the issue.

He was younger than I expected, maybe twenty-six, with a clipboard app on a cracked iPad and the practiced calm of someone who has stood in two hundred ruined basements. "This is actually pretty mild," he said, which felt like an insult at the time. Mild. There were photo albums swelling shut on a shelf four inches off the ground, close enough to soak but not to save.

We talked for a while about the sump pump, whether it had failed or simply been overwhelmed. He thought overwhelmed; the motor still hummed when he flipped the breaker. That's worse in a way — a pump that dies gives you someone to blame. A pump that just couldn't keep up means the storm gets the blame, and storms don't pay claims.

I spent that afternoon carrying boxes up the stairs two at a time, sorting as I went into three piles: save, maybe, gone. The maybe pile was the hardest. A box of my father's tax returns from the eighties. Why did I even have those? Because he gave them to me in 2003 and said keep these, and I did, and now they're pulp.

By evening the fans were running — four of them, borrowed from a neighbor, plus a dehumidifier that sounded like a small aircraft taxiing. The smell was the thing nobody warns you about. Not sewage, not quite, but something mineral and old, like a cave that had been sealed a long time and was now, reluctantly, breathing again.

Insurance paid out eleven days later. Less than the drywall alone cost. I'm not bitter about it, or I'm trying not to be, because the alternative is doing this whole thing again next spring with worse math and less patience. We raised the shelving six inches. We bought a battery backup for the pump. Small, unglamorous fixes. The kind nobody photographs for a home renovation account, but the kind that actually matter when the water decides to come back, which — everyone on this street agrees — it eventually will.
